Storytime
STOR-ee-tym
noun (Gen-Z slang)
From story time, the read-aloud hour in libraries and classrooms since the early 20th century. On YouTube in the 2010s "storytime" became a video genre: a creator, often while doing her makeup or eating, narrates a dramatic personal anecdote ("STORYTIME: my roommate stole my identity"). TikTok compressed it into one-minute and multi-part versions c. 2020, and the word now marks any narrated real-life tale online.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang a storytime is a video in which someone narrates a true (or true-ish) personal anecdote: the worst date, the wild boss, the family drama, often in parts, often while doing something else. The best are funny; many are other people’s secrets told to strangers. The Christian observation: God made us storytellers and commands the telling. "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD" (Psa 78:4). Israel’s fathers were to talk of God’s works "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way" (Deu 6:7). When Jesus delivered the man of the Gadarenes, He sent him home with one task: "tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee" (Mar 5:19) — a storytime with a commission. But the genre has a shadow. Much of it is the talebearer’s trade: a roommate, a friend, an ex, a parent laid bare for views, and "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter" (Pro 11:13). Embellishment is part of the craft, and the truth is not served by it. Paul sets the test for every story: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). A father tells his son: tell your stories — tell them well, tell them true, and tell the best one often, the story of what the Lord has done for you. But if a story is someone else’s shame, it is not yours to tell.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (YouTube 2010s, TikTok c. 2020–present, from the library story time) for a narrated personal-anecdote video — a gift of telling Scripture commands, too often spent on other people’s secrets.

expand to see more

STORYTIME, n. (Gen-Z slang, 2010s–present; YouTube and TikTok) A video in which the creator narrates a dramatic or funny personal anecdote, often in several parts. "Storytime: how I got kicked out of the library."

Often paired with another activity (makeup, cooking, driving); part 2, part 3 for serial tellings; storytime as a caption tag.

Older sense: story time, the hour when a librarian, teacher, or parent reads aloud to children.

Webster (1828), root word story: “STORY, noun [&hellip;] 1. A verbal narration or recital of a series of facts or incidents. WE observe in children a strong passion for hearing stories. 2. A written narrative of a series of facts or events. There is probably on record no story more interesting than that of Joseph in Genesis. 3. History;”

Decode for parents: ask whose story is being told; your child’s friends, siblings, and you are all possible characters.

Key Scripture

Psa 78:4 — "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."

Deu 6:7 — "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Mar 5:19 — "Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee."

Pro 11:13 — "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter."

Eph 4:29 — "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."

Modern Corruption

Storytime turns the God-given gift of telling into a trade in other people’s secrets and in drama polished for views.

expand to see more

A people who forget their stories forget their God, and Scripture is mostly story. Psalm 78 is a father’s storytime, told so the children "might set their hope in God" (Psa 78:7). A family that tells its stories at the table, including the stories of answered prayer, is obeying Deuteronomy 6:7, and a teenager who can hold a room with a well-told tale has a gift worth sharpening.

The online genre bends the gift. A storytime earns views by drama, and drama is usually someone else’s: the roommate’s meltdown, the friend’s betrayal, the parents’ divorce. The talebearer has always had an audience (Pro 11:13); now he has millions. And the craft rewards stretching the truth a little further each part. Teach your children Paul’s test, "that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29), and send them, like the healed man, home to tell "how great things the Lord hath done" (Mar 5:19).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek and Latin historia → Old French estorie → English story → library story time → 2010s YouTube and c. 2020 TikTok: storytime, the anecdote video.

2010s YouTube: STORYTIME videos, often over makeup or food

c. 2020 TikTok: multi-part storytimes
